 Key points
 The Jharkhand High Court dismissed the father-in-law's appeal against a maintenance order. 
 ₹7,000 a month goes to the widowed daughter-in-law, ₹5,000 each to her two minor sons until they attain majority. 
 The court held his age, about 84, does not exonerate his duty to maintain them. 
 Arrears must be paid within a maximum of two months from 3 November 2026. 
 Advertisement
 Ranchi, 10 November: Old age does not free a father-in-law from maintaining his widowed daughter-in-law and her two minor sons, the Jharkhand High Court has held, dismissing his appeal against a ₹17,000-a-month order.
 A Division Bench upheld the Family Court, Dhanbad’s order in full: ₹7,000 a month to the daughter-in-law and ₹5,000 each to her two sons until they attain majority. “We therefore find no merit in this appeal, and the same is accordingly dismissed; however, without costs,” the court said.
 The case
 The daughter-in-law’s husband, the appellant’s only son, died on 27 October 2020. She applied for maintenance on 24 September 2021, saying she had no independent source of livelihood and no share in his estate. The Family Court, Dhanbad decided the case on 11 June 2024; the High Court reserved the appeal on 6 October 2026 and pronounced judgment on 3 November 2026.
 What each side argued
 She alleged the father-in-law held over ₹80,00,000 in fixed deposits and earned about ₹1,00,000 a month, and sought ₹75,000 a month. He denied the fixed-deposit claim, said his retirement benefits went into building a house, and argued his only livelihood was a pension that must also keep his wife, both of them over 80 and ill. He also argued that ancestral agricultural land in which his son was a coparcener could not be the basis for maintenance.
 What the court held
 The pension, admitted at over ₹32,000 a month, was not disputed. A shop leased in his wife’s name at ₹17,000 a month since July 2017, with a 10% rise every five years — ₹18,700 since 2022, as the court worked it out — brought income that went unrebutted, putting the cumulative admitted income above ₹50,000 a month. The judges noted he had not examined himself as a witness before the Family Court.
 The court relied on the Supreme Court’s judgment in Kanchan Rai v. Geeta Sharma (2026 INSC 54), quoting its holding that “any widow of his son” in Section 21(vii) of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 cannot be read as covering only a predeceased son’s widow, and that separating widowed daughters-in-law by when the husband died would be arbitrary under Article 14. The Jharkhand court then held that “the pious responsibility of maintaining the widowed daughter-in-law and the grandchildren does not get exonerated on account of the age of the present appellant,” and that he was under a legal obligation and pious duty to maintain them.
 The Act applies to Hindus; the claim under Section 21(vii) runs only so long as she does not remarry, and the ₹5,000 for each grandson stops once he attains majority.
 Noting that no stay had been granted during the appeal and that the arrears appeared unpaid, the court directed that unpaid maintenance, running from the 24 September 2021 application, be cleared within a maximum of two months from 3 November 2026.
 Source: High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi, F.A. No. 229 of 2024 (Neutral Citation 2026:JHHC:32181-DB), judgment pronounced 3 November 2026.
